name: THE ABSENTEE SHALLOT BURGER (Comes with crispy shallots)

recipe.history:
The shallot — Allium cepa var. aggregatum — occupies a unique position in the culinary hierarchy: it is more refined than an onion, more accessible than a leek, and in the kitchens of France it is treated almost as a luxury ingredient. The shallot is believed to have originated in Central or Southwest Asia, possibly in the region around Palestine — ancient Ascalon (modern Ashkelon) in present-day Israel is sometimes cited as a point of origin, which is why one Latin name for the species is Allium ascalonicum. It spread westward through the Mediterranean and became deeply embedded in French cooking by the medieval period, particularly in Brittany and the Loire Valley, where shallot cultivation became a point of regional pride. French classical cuisine uses shallots in a way that onions cannot substitute: finely minced in beurre blanc, in mignonette sauce for oysters, in béarnaise and bordelaise, in vinaigrettes — the shallot's milder, sweeter, more wine-like flavor dissolves more gracefully into sauces than the blunter onion.

Shallots arrived in American cooking through French culinary influence, appearing first in refined restaurant kitchens in New York and New Orleans in the nineteenth century and gradually working their way into home cooking through the twentieth. Their transformation when fried is one of the great culinary revelations: thin-sliced shallot rings, dredged lightly in flour and fried in hot oil until deeply golden and crackling crisp, become something almost addictive — sweet, savory, crunchy, with a caramelized depth that raw shallot only hints at. Southeast Asian cuisines use fried shallots extensively as a finishing garnish, and this tradition was carried into American kitchens through Vietnamese, Thai, and Indonesian restaurants, which introduced food-curious Americans to the ingredient's fried potential. Burger culture met crispy shallots and immediately understood their value.

I make crispy fried shallots by the jarful and keep them on my counter. I put them on everything — soups, salads, grain bowls, eggs, braised meats. I first encountered them at a Vietnamese restaurant when I was in college: a simple bowl of pho topped with a tablespoon of crispy shallots that changed the entire texture and flavor of the dish. I went home and tried to make them immediately. My first batch burned because I didn't account for carryover cooking — shallots go from perfectly golden to scorched in about thirty seconds. The second batch I pulled just before they looked done, drained them immediately, and they finished to perfection on the paper towel. Patience, and knowing when to stop. It's a lesson that applies beyond cooking.

Crispy fried shallots are textural perfection on a burger — they add crunch, sweetness, and savory depth simultaneously. But they need a partner capable of matching their intensity, and only a medium-rare patty provides that. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the beef patty is still juicy, its fat still present and liquid, providing the moisture and richness that the crispy shallots play against. An overcooked patty loses this moisture and richness, and the crispy shallots become nothing more than a garnish on a dry protein. Medium rare is not optional here — it is the architectural decision upon which the entire burger's balance depends.
ingredients: 6 large shallots, peeled and very thinly sliced into rings (use a mandoline if available)
Neutral oil (canola or vegetable) for frying, enough to fill a small pot 2 inches deep
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead on medium 8 minutes. Transfer to oiled bowl, cover, rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled. Shape into 4 balls, proof on a parchment-lined sheet 45 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.

2. Make the shallot-herb aioli: Whisk egg yolks, vinegar, and Dijon in a bowl. Drizzle in oil in a very slow, thin stream while whisking constantly until emulsified and thick. Fold in minced shallot, thyme, chives, and salt. Refrigerate at least 30 minutes.

3. Make the crispy shallots: Soak the sliced shallot rings in milk for 15 minutes. Combine flour, salt, and cayenne in a shallow bowl. Fill a small heavy pot with 2 inches of neutral oil. Heat to 350°F (175°C). Drain shallots and toss in the seasoned flour, shaking off excess. Fry in batches — do not crowd — stirring occasionally, 3 to 4 minutes until golden and crispy. Watch carefully: they go from golden to burned quickly. Transfer immediately to a paper-towel-lined plate and sprinkle lightly with sea salt. They will crisp further as they cool.

4. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form each into a patty 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Make a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and onion powder just before cooking.

5. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties 3 minutes undisturbed. Flip and place a slice of Gruyère on each. Cook 2 to 2.5 minutes more until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). Remove and rest 3 minutes.
6. Toast bun cut sides in the residual skillet fat over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds.

7. Assemble: Spread shallot-herb aioli generously on both cut bun surfaces. Place a leaf of butter lettuce on the bottom bun. Set the rested patty with melted Gruyère on the lettuce. Add tomato slices. Pile a generous mound of crispy fried shallots on top — this should be dramatic and abundant. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately while shallots are still crisp.
